name: com.seeksat/seeksat
title: SeekSat
description: Satellite passes, live positions, visibility, clouds, radio Doppler and launches. Free, no key.

tools.name: list_satellites
tools.description: SeekSat's ten popular satellites (ISS, Tiangong, Hubble, weather satellites and a few others): always all ten, in a fixed order, with aliases, page url and orbit data freshness. Not the full list: every other tool accepts any NORAD catalog number. To find another satellite by name use search_satellites; for one satellite's facts and TLE use get_satellite. Takes no input, reads only SeekSat's own catalog and does not fail. Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address.

tools.name: find_passes
tools.description:
Upcoming passes of one satellite or several over a location within windowHours (default 48, or 72 with limit; up to 240), in time order and not ranked: limit 1 for "when is the next pass?", no limit for the full schedule ("when does it pass this week?"). Which pass tool: find_passes lists passes in time order, from the next one (limit 1) to every pass in the window; find_best_pass ranks them by rating, for one satellite or, with none named, from a scan of many ("what can I see tonight?"); get_radio_pass gives one pass's Doppler and tuning, the next one by default. chart:true also draws the first pass listed as a sky chart (the image get_pass_chart gives) in this same result, so one call answers when and where to look. For another pass's chart give its peak time to get_pass_chart; to check clouds give it to get_pass_weather.

With a list of up to 10 satellites the result is one combined schedule: each pass also names its satellite, and satellites has one entry per satellite (one that can't be found gets an error there; the others still answer). Duplicates are listed once, and limit counts passes across the whole list. One satellite, not in a list, puts satellite, noradId and url at the top.

mode "visual" (default) keeps only the part of each pass that can be seen by eye, so rise and set can fall mid-sky and the peak is the highest point of that part; mode "radio" keeps the whole pass above minElevation. Rise and set are where it crosses minElevation, not the horizon, so a higher minElevation gives shorter, fewer passes. In visual mode the cloud forecast for the place is folded into the ratings.

rating is the one seeksat.com shows. Visual mode: how much brighter than the faintest visible star for skyType the pass gets (headroomMag), a level lower for some forecast cloud and one bar for a cloudy forecast, up to 4 days ahead; at most Fair when the brightness is estimated or the peak is below 15 degrees, at most Good below 25 degrees or when seen for under 90 seconds, and Excellent only above 40 degrees. Radio mode: the peak height, a bar lower for each 6 dB of extra path loss beyond 2,000 km, and at most Fair when SatNOGS stations tried at least 3 times in 30 days and heard nothing.

An empty list comes with a note saying why (it never rises high enough from that latitude, the sky never gets dark, and so on); when the next pass is further off, give a longer windowHours. Each pass is about 1 KB. SeekSat keeps nothing between calls (no saved places, lists or alerts), so give the place every time; for a reminder, give the user passUrl, which opens the pass on seeksat.com, where Remind me alerts them before it starts. Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change. A place name is looked up with OpenStreetMap (one lookup a second, cached), which can add a few seconds; lat and lon or a grid square need none. Cloud forecasts are cached for 10 minutes per area. Over 72 hours (unless limit is 5 or less), with more than one satellite, or with chart:true it is a heavy call: one at a time per caller; another waits up to 20 seconds, then is refused as busy.

satellite.description: NORAD catalog number (as a number or a string) or a name, e.g. 25544, "25544" or "iss"; or a list of up to 10, e.g. [25544, 48274], for one schedule of all their passes.

lat.description: observer latitude in decimal degrees, north positive (-90 to 90). Give it with lon, or give location instead.

lon.description: observer longitude in decimal degrees, east positive and west negative (-180 to 180).

location.description: where the observer is, when lat and lon are not given (they win when both are): a Maidenhead grid square (EN52, EN52ve, EN52ve12), coordinates in any common form ("41.88, -87.63", "41.88N 87.63W", "41°52'48"N 87°37'48"W", a Google Maps link or geo: URI), read locally, or a place name (city, address, landmark) looked up with OpenStreetMap.

windowHours.description: how far ahead to look, in hours, up to 240 (10 days). Default 48, or 72 with limit.

minElevation.description: lowest elevation that counts: a pass must climb above it, and rise and set are when it crosses it, in degrees above the horizon (0 to 90). Default 10.

mode.description: "visual" (default): naked-eye passes, sunlit while the sky is dark; "radio": every line-of-sight pass, day or night.

skyType.description: how dark the observer's sky is, for the visual rating as on seeksat.com: "city" (stars to magnitude 3.5), "suburban" (stars to magnitude 4.5), "rural" (stars to magnitude 5.5), "dark" (stars to magnitude 6.5). Default "suburban".

limit.description: return only the first limit passes in time order, 1 to 100: 1 for the next pass. Default: every pass in the window.

chart.description: true to also render the first pass's polar sky chart (PNG, 800 by 897 pixels, about 120 KB) and return it in this same result. Default false.

tools.name: get_position
tools.description:
Where a satellite is now, or at a given time: the point on Earth straight below it, its altitude, whether it is sunlit, and its page url. For every satellite in the sky right now use find_satellites_up_now; for when it passes over use find_passes; for its orbit and TLE use get_satellite.

With a place (lat and lon, or location) it also gives where the satellite is in that place's sky (azimuth, apparent elevation, range and whether it is above the horizon), and the place sets the time zone for local times and for reading a time with no offset; without one, times are UTC.

With durationMinutes it also gives the ground track from that time on, one point every stepSeconds (up to a day, at most 720 points of about 0.3 KB each), with the sky fields too when a place is given. lonDeg jumps between 180 and -180 at the antimeridian, so split a drawn line there.

With a list of up to 10 satellites ("where are the ISS and Tiangong now?") it gives where each is at that one moment: positions has one entry per satellite with its name, noradId, url and the fields above (one that can't be found or worked out gets an error there; the others still answer), and time, resolvedLocation and interpretedAs stay at the top. Duplicates are listed once. A ground track takes one satellite, not a list.

A time more than 30 days from the orbital elements' epoch is refused. Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change. A place name is looked up with OpenStreetMap (one lookup a second, cached), which can add a few seconds; lat and lon or a grid square need none. With more than one satellite it is a heavy call: one at a time per caller; another waits up to 20 seconds, then is refused as busy.

satellite.description: NORAD catalog number (as a number or a string) or a name, e.g. 25544, "25544" or "iss"; or a list of up to 10, e.g. [25544, 48274], for where each is at the same moment (no ground track with a list).

time.description: when (with durationMinutes, where the track starts). Default: now. ISO 8601 with Z or an offset, e.g. "2026-11-14T21:00:00-06:00"; a time with no offset, e.g. "2026-11-14T21:00", is read in the observer's time zone, and the result echoes how it was read (interpretedAs). A local time the clocks skip at a daylight-saving change is moved forward, with a note.

durationMinutes.description: how long a ground track to return, in minutes from time, up to 1440 (a day); about 93 is one ISS orbit. Omit for one position.

stepSeconds.description: seconds between track points, 10 to 3600. Default 60, or wider when needed to keep the track to 720 points; a step you give that would make more is refused, naming the smallest that fits.

lat.description: observer latitude in decimal degrees, north positive (-90 to 90). Give it with lon, or give location instead.

lon.description: observer longitude in decimal degrees, east positive and west negative (-180 to 180).

location.description: where the observer is, when lat and lon are not given (they win when both are): a Maidenhead grid square (EN52, EN52ve, EN52ve12), coordinates in any common form ("41.88, -87.63", "41.88N 87.63W", "41°52'48"N 87°37'48"W", a Google Maps link or geo: URI), read locally, or a place name (city, address, landmark) looked up with OpenStreetMap. Optional here: with it, the result adds azimuth and elevation from there.

tools.name: get_pass_weather
tools.description:
Cloud-cover forecast (Open-Meteo and MET Norway) and the chance of a clear view for a location at one time, such as a pass's peak. The forecast reaches about 7 to 16 days ahead, and viewingProbability is blended toward 0.5 the further ahead the time is, since forecasts lose skill.

It knows nothing about satellites: give the place a pass was found for and that pass's peak time from find_passes or find_best_pass. In visual mode those already fold the forecast into their ratings, so call this to show the cloud numbers or to check another time. With no forecast for that time (in the past, beyond the forecast, a time it cannot read, or a failed fetch), available is false with a reason, never a stand-in number.

Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change. A place name is looked up with OpenStreetMap (one lookup a second, cached), which can add a few seconds; lat and lon or a grid square need none. Forecasts are cached for 10 minutes per area (rounded to about 11 km), and a fetch gives up after 8 seconds.

lon.description: observer longitude in decimal degrees, east positive and west negative (-180 to 180).

A local time the clocks skip at a daylight-saving change is moved forward, with a note.

tools.name: get_pass_chart
tools.description: Render a polar sky chart of a satellite's pass over a location: where to look, with the moon, planets and stars in place. Returns the charted pass (the same row find_passes gives) and a one-line summary as JSON, then the image, a PNG of 800 by 897 pixels, about 120 KB. By default it charts the next pass; give time (a pass's rise or peak from find_passes or find_best_pass) to chart that pass, with the same minElevation it came from. A geostationary satellite has no passes: stationary says where to point instead, with no image. A time more than 30 days from the orbital elements' epoch is refused. tools.name: get_satellite
tools.description:
Facts about one satellite, for "what is this satellite?" or to get its TLE: a plain-words summary, object type, owner, launch and re-entry, orbit, size, radio downlinks and its current orbital elements (TLE lines, or OMM past NORAD 99999) with their age, and launchUrl, the page of the launch that put it up, for launches since October 2026 (get_launch takes it for the launch's details). It takes no location or time: for where it is use get_position, for when to see it use find_passes or find_best_pass, and for a pass's Doppler and reception use get_radio_pass.

Owner, launch and type come from CelesTrak's satellite catalog and are null when it does not say; orbit is null once it has re-entered. Outside the popular list a name resolves only on an exact whole-name match, so prefer NORAD numbers from search_satellites.

Most satellites come from SeekSat's own copy of the catalog, refreshed every four hours; one missing from it is fetched from CelesTrak, which can take a few seconds and is limited per hour. Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change.

satellite.description: NORAD catalog number (as a number or a string) or a name, e.g. 25544, "25544" or "iss".

tools.name: search_satellites
tools.description:
Search the full satellite catalog by name, alias or NORAD number, best match first, to turn a name like "SDO" or "NOAA 19" into a NORAD number for the other tools (they resolve a name outside the popular list only on an exact whole-name match). For the popular satellites use list_satellites; for one satellite's facts and TLE use get_satellite.

Matching order: an exact NORAD number, the whole name, the start of the name or of a word, part of the number, anywhere in the name, then near misses, so a small typo still finds it. To find satellites by downlink kind, use mode "radio" with the kind as the query (query "sstv"). No match is an empty list. Reads only SeekSat's catalog. Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change.

query.description: a name, part of one, or a NORAD number, e.g. "sdo", "noaa 19", "25544". With mode "radio", a downlink kind as the whole query (e.g. "sstv", "aprs", "cw") lists satellites that have one.

limit.description: how many results to return, 1 to 20. Default 10.

mode.description: "visual" (default): best name match first; "radio": satellites with known radio downlinks first among equally good matches. To list satellites with a kind of downlink, set mode "radio" and put the kind in query (e.g. query "sstv"); mode itself takes only "visual" or "radio".

tools.name: get_radio_pass
tools.description:
Radio details for one pass of a satellite over a location: its known downlink (and uplink) frequencies, the Doppler swing, when to tune to what (at 10 and 30 degrees up and at closest approach), and a table of at most 40 evenly spaced rows for pointing an antenna and tuning a radio. To choose a satellite or pass first use find_best_pass with mode radio, or find_passes; for a sky chart of the pass use get_pass_chart.

It uses the first pass that climbs above minElevation within windowHours (default 48), or with time the pass peaking nearest it (past or future, within 30 days of the elements' epoch). If there is none, window is null and message says why; the downlinks are still listed. A satellite that never sets here (geosynchronous) gets the next 24 hours instead. frequencyMHz picks the downlink; by default it is the one SatNOGS stations heard most recently, else the catalog's.

Predictions come from published elements: the transmitter's own offset is unknown, so compare the curve's shape. passUrl opens this pass on seeksat.com on the same frequency, and its Radio chart downloads the full table as CSV. Reception data is from SatNOGS Network (CC BY-SA 4.0). Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change. A place name is looked up with OpenStreetMap (one lookup a second, cached), which can add a few seconds; lat and lon or a grid square need none.

satellite.description: NORAD catalog number (as a number or a string) or a name, e.g. 25544, "25544" or "iss". e.g. "so-50" or 27607.

lat.description: observer latitude in decimal degrees, north positive (-90 to 90). Give it with lon, or give location instead.

lon.description: observer longitude in decimal degrees, east positive and west negative (-180 to 180).

location.description: where the observer is, when lat and lon are not given (they win when both are): a Maidenhead grid square (EN52, EN52ve, EN52ve12), coordinates in any common form ("41.88, -87.63", "41.88N 87.63W", "41°52'48"N 87°37'48"W", a Google Maps link or geo: URI), read locally, or a place name (city, address, landmark) looked up with OpenStreetMap.

frequencyMHz.description: the downlink to compute Doppler for, in MHz. Default: the satellite's default known downlink.

time.description: a time near the wanted pass's peak (e.g. from find_passes), past or future. Default: the next pass. ISO 8601 with Z or an offset, e.g. "2026-11-14T21:00:00-06:00"; a time with no offset, e.g. "2026-11-14T21:00", is read in the observer's time zone, and the result echoes how it was read (interpretedAs). A local time the clocks skip at a daylight-saving change is moved forward, with a note.

minElevation.description: lowest elevation that counts: a pass must climb above it, and rise and set are when it crosses it, in degrees above the horizon (0 to 90). Default 10.

windowHours.description: how far ahead to look, in hours, up to 240 (10 days). Default 48. How far past the start to look for a pass.

tools.name: find_best_pass
tools.description:
The best upcoming passes over a location, ranked by the rating seeksat.com shows ("what's the best pass tonight?"): best is the top pass and passes the top limit (default 3, up to 20), each naming its satellite. Which pass tool: find_passes lists passes in time order, from the next one (limit 1) to every pass in the window; find_best_pass ranks them by rating, for one satellite or, with none named, from a scan of many ("what can I see tonight?"); get_radio_pass gives one pass's Doppler and tuning, the next one by default. For what is up at this moment use find_satellites_up_now; to draw the winning pass set chart:true, or give a pass's peak time to get_pass_chart.

What it searches. With satellite: that satellite's passes, the top limit and not every pass. Without, a scan: visual mode (default) covers the popular satellites plus CelesTrak's visual group of the brightest objects, over 72 hours (up to 168); radio mode covers every satellite with known downlinks over 24 hours (up to 72), optionally only those with a downlink in bands or of a kind in modes. A scan leaves out satellites whose elements are more than 14 days old and counts what it skipped.

mode "visual" (default) keeps only the part of each pass that can be seen by eye, so rise and set can fall mid-sky and the peak is the highest point of that part; mode "radio" keeps the whole pass above minElevation. Rise and set are where it crosses minElevation, not the horizon, so a higher minElevation gives shorter, fewer passes.

rating is the one seeksat.com shows. Visual mode: how much brighter than the faintest visible star for skyType the pass gets (headroomMag), a level lower for some forecast cloud and one bar for a cloudy forecast, up to 4 days ahead; at most Fair when the brightness is estimated or the peak is below 15 degrees, at most Good below 25 degrees or when seen for under 90 seconds, and Excellent only above 40 degrees. Radio mode: the peak height, a bar lower for each 6 dB of extra path loss beyond 2,000 km, and at most Fair when SatNOGS stations tried at least 3 times in 30 days and heard nothing.

Ranking. Visual: rating bars, then a measured brightness before an estimated one, then headroomMag, then captureProbability, with the cloud forecast folded in where it reaches. Radio scans: satellites a hobby receiver can tune (30 MHz to 1 GHz) first unless bands is given, then rating bars, then how recently SatNOGS stations heard it (48 hours, 7 days, 30 days, unknown, probably silent), then how often, then peak elevation, then captureProbability. Unknown reception never holds a satellite down. Reception data is from SatNOGS Network (CC BY-SA 4.0).

An empty result comes with a note saying why. Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change. A place name is looked up with OpenStreetMap (one lookup a second, cached), which can add a few seconds; lat and lon or a grid square need none. Cloud forecasts are cached for 10 minutes per area. A heavy call: one at a time per caller; another waits up to 20 seconds, then is refused as busy.

satellite.description: NORAD catalog number (as a number or a string) or a name, e.g. 25544, "25544" or "iss". Omit to scan: visual mode scans the popular satellites plus CelesTrak's visual group, radio mode every satellite with known downlinks.

lat.description: observer latitude in decimal degrees, north positive (-90 to 90). Give it with lon, or give location instead.

lon.description: observer longitude in decimal degrees, east positive and west negative (-180 to 180).

location.description: where the observer is, when lat and lon are not given (they win when both are): a Maidenhead grid square (EN52, EN52ve, EN52ve12), coordinates in any common form ("41.88, -87.63", "41.88N 87.63W", "41°52'48"N 87°37'48"W", a Google Maps link or geo: URI), read locally, or a place name (city, address, landmark) looked up with OpenStreetMap.

windowHours.description: how far ahead to look, in hours, up to 240 (10 days). Default 72. With no satellite named, a visual scan stops at 168, and a radio scan defaults to 24 and stops at 72.

minElevation.description: lowest elevation that counts: a pass must climb above it, and rise and set are when it crosses it, in degrees above the horizon (0 to 90). Default 10.

limit.description: how many ranked passes to return, 1 to 20. Default 3.

mode.description: "visual" (default): naked-eye passes, sunlit while the sky is dark; "radio": every line-of-sight pass, day or night.

skyType.description: how dark the observer's sky is, for the visual rating as on seeksat.com: "city" (stars to magnitude 3.5), "suburban" (stars to magnitude 4.5), "rural" (stars to magnitude 5.5), "dark" (stars to magnitude 6.5). Default "suburban".

bands.description: radio scan only: keep satellites with a downlink in these bands: hf (3-30 MHz), wx (137 MHz weather), 2m (144-148 MHz), 70cm (420-450 MHz), l (1-2 GHz), s (2-4 GHz), other. Default: any band.

modes.description: radio scan only: keep satellites with a downlink of one of these kinds, matched on its mode or label, e.g. ["fm", "apt", "sstv"]. Default: any.

chart.description: true to also render the winning pass's polar sky chart (PNG, 800 by 897 pixels, about 120 KB) and return it in this same result. Default false.

tools.name: find_satellites_up_now
tools.description:
What is in the sky over a location right now, from every satellite in the catalog (active satellites plus CelesTrak's visual group). For upcoming passes use find_best_pass or find_passes; for one satellite at any time, get_position with a place.

mode "visual" (default): sunlit satellites above minElevation while the sky is dark there (the Sun more than about 6 degrees down), brightest first; magnitudes are measured for most bright satellites (McCants' observations) and estimated for the rest. mode "radio": satellites with known downlinks above minElevation, day or night, those a hobby receiver can tune (30 MHz to 1 GHz) first, then the most recently heard by SatNOGS, then the highest.

Up to limit (default 10, up to 50). Satellites whose elements are more than 14 days from now are left out and counted. Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change. A place name is looked up with OpenStreetMap (one lookup a second, cached), which can add a few seconds; lat and lon or a grid square need none. A heavy call: one at a time per caller; another waits up to 20 seconds, then is refused as busy.

lat.description: observer latitude in decimal degrees, north positive (-90 to 90). Give it with lon, or give location instead.

lon.description: observer longitude in decimal degrees, east positive and west negative (-180 to 180).

location.description: where the observer is, when lat and lon are not given (they win when both are): a Maidenhead grid square (EN52, EN52ve, EN52ve12), coordinates in any common form ("41.88, -87.63", "41.88N 87.63W", "41°52'48"N 87°37'48"W", a Google Maps link or geo: URI), read locally, or a place name (city, address, landmark) looked up with OpenStreetMap.

mode.description: "visual" (default): sunlit satellites in a dark sky, brightest first; "radio": satellites with known downlinks, day or night: those a hobby receiver can tune first, then the most recently heard, then the highest.

minElevation.description: lowest elevation to list, in degrees above the horizon (0 to 90). Default 10.

limit.description: how many satellites to return, 1 to 50. Default 10.

tools.name: identify_satellite
tools.description:
"What was that moving light?" Given where and when a light was seen, lists the satellites that were sunlit, above the horizon and within tolerance degrees of that spot, best match first, from every satellite in the catalog. For satellites up at this moment use find_satellites_up_now; for upcoming passes use find_passes or find_best_pass.

A match must lie within tolerance of the reported spot (azimuth or direction, plus elevation). travel never adds a match; it only re-ranks them by how well each one's direction of travel agrees. Sightings by eye are often 10 to 20 degrees off, so widen tolerance before concluding nothing matched.

It needs the Sun at least about 3 degrees below the horizon: if the sky was too bright, a note says so instead of a list, and with no match a note suggests checking the time and direction or widening tolerance. Satellites whose elements are more than 14 days from the sighting are left out and counted. Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change. A place name is looked up with OpenStreetMap (one lookup a second, cached), which can add a few seconds; lat and lon or a grid square need none. A heavy call: one at a time per caller; another waits up to 20 seconds, then is refused as busy.

lat.description: observer latitude in decimal degrees, north positive (-90 to 90). Give it with lon, or give location instead.

lon.description: observer longitude in decimal degrees, east positive and west negative (-180 to 180).

location.description: where the observer is, when lat and lon are not given (they win when both are): a Maidenhead grid square (EN52, EN52ve, EN52ve12), coordinates in any common form ("41.88, -87.63", "41.88N 87.63W", "41°52'48"N 87°37'48"W", a Google Maps link or geo: URI), read locally, or a place name (city, address, landmark) looked up with OpenStreetMap.

time.description: time of the sighting. Default: now. ISO 8601 with Z or an offset, e.g. "2026-11-14T21:00:00-06:00"; a time with no offset, e.g. "2026-11-14T21:00", is read in the observer's time zone, and the result echoes how it was read (interpretedAs). A local time the clocks skip at a daylight-saving change is moved forward, with a note.

azimuth.description: where it was, in degrees from north (90 = east), 0 to 360. Give this or direction.

direction.description: where it was, as a compass word: N, NNE, NE, ... or "north-east".

elevation.description: how high it was, in degrees above the horizon (0 to 90, 90 = straight up). Required.

travel.description: the compass direction it was moving towards, e.g. "NE". Optional, but it sharpens the match.

tolerance.description: how far off the reported spot a match may be, in degrees, 1 to 45. Default 10.

limit.description: how many candidates to return, 1 to 10. Default 5.

tools.name: find_launches
tools.description:
Upcoming or recent rocket launches worldwide ("when is the next launch?", "what launched this week?", "any launches from Florida soon?"). when "upcoming" (default) lists launches still to come, soonest first, up to days ahead (default 14); "recent" lists flown launches, newest first, up to days back (default 7; history starts in October 2026). For the next launch use limit 1. For one launch's crew, boosters, pad forecast, updates and the satellites it put in orbit, pass its launchUrl or id to get_launch.

Filters, all optional, combine: name (the mission, for "when is Artemis II?"), provider, rocket and site each match part of the name, ignoring case; status (go, tbd and hold go with upcoming; in-flight, success and failure with recent; a mismatch is an error); crewed; and a place (lat and lon, or location) keeps pads within radiusKm (default 1500) and adds distanceKm. Distance is not visibility: nothing here says whether a launch can be seen from a place.

net is null when only the day is set (see timeKnown). Times have a <name>Local twin on the place's clock, else the pad's. Each launch carries launchUrl, its seeksat.com page with a live countdown, and is about 1 KB. An empty list comes with a note. Data: Launch Library 2 (The Space Devs), stored by SeekSat and refreshed about every 15 minutes, never fetched per call; show the source field as credit. SeekSat knows upcoming launches with a firm day or time (not ones set only to a month or year), and flown ones from October 2026 on. Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change. A place name is looked up with OpenStreetMap (one lookup a second, cached), which can add a few seconds; lat and lon or a grid square need none.

when.description: "upcoming" (default): launches still to come, soonest first; "recent": launches that have flown, newest first.

days.description: how many days ahead (upcoming) or back (recent) to look, 1 to 90. Default 14 upcoming, 7 recent.

name.description: the mission, matched as part of its name, e.g. "Artemis", "Crew-13", "Starlink Group 10".

provider.description: launch provider, matched as part of the name, e.g. "SpaceX", "Rocket Lab", "CASC".

rocket.description: rocket, matched as part of the name, e.g. "Falcon 9", "Electron", "Long March".

site.description: launch site or pad, matched as part of the name, e.g. "Cape Canaveral", "Kennedy", "Vandenberg", "Baikonur".

status.description: keep only this status: "go", "tbd" (time or day not yet confirmed), "hold" (these three with when "upcoming"), "in-flight", "success", "failure" (with partial failures; these three with when "recent"). A status that cannot occur for when is an error.

crewed.description: true: only launches with people on board; false: only uncrewed ones.

lat.description: observer latitude in decimal degrees, north positive (-90 to 90). Give it with lon, or give location instead.

lon.description: observer longitude in decimal degrees, east positive and west negative (-180 to 180).

location.description: where the observer is, when lat and lon are not given (they win when both are): a Maidenhead grid square (EN52, EN52ve, EN52ve12), coordinates in any common form ("41.88, -87.63", "41.88N 87.63W", "41°52'48"N 87°37'48"W", a Google Maps link or geo: URI), read locally, or a place name (city, address, landmark) looked up with OpenStreetMap. Optional here: with it, only launches from pads within radiusKm are kept.

radiusKm.description: with a place: how far its pads may be, in km, up to 20000. Default 1500. With no place it is an error.

limit.description: how many launches to return, 1 to 50. Default 10.

tools.name: get_launch
tools.description:
One launch in full, by its launchUrl, slug or id (from find_launches, or launchUrl from get_satellite): crew, spacecraft, boosters and landings, the range's weather go chance and concerns, padWeather (the forecast at the pad for liftoff, within about 9 days, from Open-Meteo and MET Norway), delayReason when the date slipped, failReason, the latest updates, and Launch Library's description.

For a flown launch, objects lists what it put in orbit with NORAD numbers, ready for find_passes, get_position or get_satellite ("when can I see the Starlinks launched yesterday?"). New objects usually reach the catalog within about 3 days; until then, and for a failed or suborbital launch, a note says why the list is empty. It never says whether a launch can be seen from a place.

Times are UTC with a <name>Local twin on the pad's clock; net is null when only the day is set (see timeKnown). A launch it does not know is a not-found error. The result is about 2 to 3 KB. Data: Launch Library 2 (The Space Devs), stored by SeekSat and refreshed about every 15 minutes, never fetched per call; show the source field as credit. SeekSat knows upcoming launches with a firm day or time (not ones set only to a month or year), and flown ones from October 2026 on. Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change.

launch.description: the launch: its launchUrl (e.g. "https://seeksat.com/launches/starlink-group-10-30"), its slug ("starlink-group-10-30") or its id, from find_launches.
